questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 5 days of fever, sore throat, myalgias, and a faint macular rash over his trunk. He reports condomless sex with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. Temperature is 38.6 C (101.5 F). He has tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory testing follows the standard serum algorithm:

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?
choices: Repeat the combination immunoassay in 3 months
Measure the CD4 T-cell count
Send an HIV-1 nucleic acid test on plasma
Report the result as HIV-2 infection
Order a phenotypic tropism assay on the plasma sample

explain.html:
The CDC fourth-generation algorithm starts with an HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay. A nonreactive screen means no HIV-1 or HIV-2 antibodies and no p24 antigen. A reactive screen goes to an HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay, which can show HIV-1 antibodies, HIV-2 antibodies, or both. When the differentiation assay is HIV-1 negative or indeterminate with HIV-2 negative, the tie is broken by an HIV-1 nucleic acid test (NAT): a positive NAT means acute HIV-1 infection and a negative NAT means no HIV-1.

This man has the acute retroviral syndrome (fever, pharyngitis, rash, lymphadenopathy) 3 weeks after a high-risk exposure. His screen is reactive because the fourth-generation test also detects p24 antigen, while his antibodies are not yet mature enough to read clearly on the differentiation assay, which is the seroconversion window. Sending HIV-1 NAT now confirms the diagnosis at the moment viral load and transmission risk are highest, so treatment and counseling are not delayed.
explain.table:
Ag/Ab screenDifferentiation assayInterpretation
NonreactiveNot doneNegative for HIV-1/2 antibodies and p24 antigen
ReactiveHIV-1 positive, HIV-2 negativeHIV-1 antibodies detected
ReactiveHIV-1 negative, HIV-2 positiveHIV-2 antibodies detected
ReactiveHIV-1 and HIV-2 positiveHIV antibodies detected
ReactiveHIV-1 negative or indeterminate, HIV-2 negativeHIV-1 NAT: positive = acute HIV-1; negative = no HIV-1
why: Waiting months leaves a likely acute infection undiagnosed during peak infectiousness when NAT can answer the question today.
A CD4 count stages immune damage but cannot confirm or exclude HIV infection.
HIV-2 was nonreactive on the differentiation assay, so nothing points to HIV-2.
Tropism testing decides whether a CCR5 antagonist can be used; it plays no part in diagnosis.
explain.takeaway: A reactive fourth-generation Ag/Ab screen with an HIV-1 negative or indeterminate differentiation assay is resolved by HIV-1 NAT, which detects acute infection before antibodies are fully formed.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To develop familiarity with the different methods used to diagnose HIV infection

questions.stem:
Two untreated men with chronic HIV infection, both 35 years old and asymptomatic, are seen in clinic on the same day. Their baseline results are:

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following statements best describes the expected course over the next several years if neither is treated?
choices: Both have the same risk because their CD4 counts are similar
Patient 1 has the higher risk because his virus replicates more slowly
Neither is at risk until the CD4 count drops below 500/mm3
Patient 2 will progress to AIDS more quickly than Patient 1
Risk cannot be judged without a phenotypic resistance assay

explain.html:
Untreated HIV follows a predictable course: a burst of viremia at primary infection, a set point during years of clinical latency, and a steady decline in CD4 cells until opportunistic diseases appear. Two markers describe that course differently. The CD4 count shows how much immune damage has already happened, while the plasma viral load shows how fast the virus is driving the decline. In the Mellors cohort, patients with baseline CD4 counts above 500 separated sharply by viral load stratum, and within any CD4 band the risk of AIDS at 3, 6 and 9 years rose with viral load.

These two men have nearly identical CD4 counts, so their current damage is the same. Patient 2's viral load of 95,000 copies/mL puts him in the highest stratum, so he is expected to reach AIDS much sooner than Patient 1 at 350 copies/mL. This is why viral load predicts progression and is followed alongside the CD4 count.
explain.table:
MarkerWhat it tells youUse
CD4 countCurrent immune damageStaging; AIDS when below 200
Plasma viral loadRate of viral replicationPredicts speed of progression; marks treatment response
why: Similar CD4 counts reflect similar current damage, not similar speed of future decline.
A lower viral load means slower progression, so Patient 1 has the lower risk.
Viral load predicts progression even when the CD4 count is above 500, as the cohort data show.
Resistance testing guides drug choice and does not stage untreated natural history.
explain.takeaway: In untreated HIV the CD4 count measures current immune damage, while the plasma viral load predicts how fast the patient will progress to AIDS.
explain.topic: Viral load and CD4 as prognostic markers
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the natural history of HIV-1 infection and transmission risk

rows.if_right: two patients matched for both CD4 count and viral load

rows.why: A lower viral load means slower progression, so Patient 1 has the lower risk.
rows.if_right: Patient 1 having the higher viral load, which would predict faster progression

rows.why: Viral load predicts progression even when the CD4 count is above 500, as the cohort data show.
rows.if_right: a patient whose CD4 count has fallen below 200, the threshold for stage 3 (AIDS)

rows.if_right: a patient failing therapy who needs a new regimen chosen

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman comes to a primary care clinic for a routine physical before starting a new job. She has been in a monogamous relationship for 4 years, has never used injection drugs, and has never received blood products. She has no symptoms. She has never been tested for HIV. Physical examination is normal.

Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to HIV testing in this patient?
choices: No testing, because she reports no risk factors
Testing only after a separate signed HIV consent form
Testing only if she reports a new sexual partner
Routine testing with notification that she may decline
Testing deferred until she becomes pregnant or develops an STD

explain.html:
CDC recommends routine voluntary HIV testing for everyone aged 13 to 64 in health care settings, and the recommendation is not based on patient risk. The model is opt-out: the patient is told the test will be done and may decline, and no separate consent for HIV is needed. Pregnant women, patients with an STD and patients with active tuberculosis should all be screened, and repeat testing is left to the provider based on risk. The reason is that a meaningful share of people with HIV do not know they are infected, and that unaware group accounts for a disproportionate share of new infections.

This 24-year-old has no reported risk factors and has never been tested, but her age alone places her in the screening group. The right approach is to tell her an HIV test is part of routine care and that she may decline. Finding infections early leads to timely treatment and a public health benefit.
why: Screening for ages 13 to 64 does not depend on reported risk.
The CDC model requires no separate signed consent for HIV testing.
A first screen is indicated now; risk only guides whether to repeat it.
Pregnancy and STDs are additional reasons to screen, not prerequisites.
explain.takeaway: CDC recommends routine opt-out HIV screening for all patients aged 13 to 64 in health care settings, without separate consent and regardless of risk.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To describe current recommendations for HIV testing and the use of laboratory markers in patient management

rows.if_right: a patient outside the 13 to 64 range with no risk factors or other indication

rows.if_right: a setting whose own law still required written HIV-specific consent

rows.if_right: a patient already screened once, where the question is when to repeat

rows.why: Pregnancy and STDs are additional reasons to screen, not prerequisites.
rows.if_right: a patient outside the age range who is now pregnant or has an STD

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old man is diagnosed with HIV infection after a routine screening test. He feels well and has had no opportunistic infections, unexplained weight loss, or malignancies. Examination is normal except for mild generalized lymphadenopathy.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following best describes this patient's disease stage?
choices: Acute HIV infection, because he has lymphadenopathy
Clinical latency, because he has no opportunistic illness
AIDS, based on the CD4 count alone
AIDS only once an AIDS-defining infection develops
Stage 2 infection, because the viral load is under 500,000 copies/mL

explain.html:
Without therapy, HIV causes a steady decline in CD4 cells over years, and the risk of opportunistic infection rises as the count falls, especially below 200. AIDS marks severe immunodeficiency, usually from late untreated infection. It can be reached two ways: an AIDS-defining illness (most are opportunistic infections), or a CD4 count alone, since by definition a CD4 count below 200 is AIDS (stage 3, systemic immunodeficiency).

This man feels well and has no opportunistic illness, but his CD4 count of 170 meets the definition by itself. His high viral load says the decline is active but does not set the stage. Recognizing AIDS by the count matters because his risk of opportunistic infection is already high even though he has no symptoms.
explain.table:
PhaseTypical features
Acute (primary) infectionWeeks after exposure: fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy; very high viremia
Clinical latencyYears, few symptoms, steady CD4 decline
AIDS (stage 3)CD4 below 200 or an AIDS-defining illness
why: Acute infection is a febrile illness within weeks of exposure, not asymptomatic disease with a low CD4 count.
Being asymptomatic does not exclude AIDS when the CD4 count is below 200.
An AIDS-defining illness is one route to the diagnosis, but a CD4 count below 200 is enough by itself.
Staging uses the CD4 count; viral load does not set the stage.
explain.takeaway: A CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3 defines AIDS (stage 3) even in a patient with no opportunistic infection.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the natural history of HIV-1 infection and transmission risk

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV infection is starting treatment. He has had intolerance to several medications in the past, and his physician is considering a regimen that includes a drug that blocks the viral coreceptor CCR5 on the host cell. Baseline CBC, chemistries, hepatitis serologies, and a genotypic resistance test have already been sent.

Which additional laboratory test must be done before this drug can be prescribed?
choices: HLA-B*5701 genotype
Viral tropism assay
Plasma p24 antigen level
Interferon-gamma release assay
Repeat fourth-generation immunoassay

explain.html:
A newly diagnosed patient gets a standard baseline panel: CBC, CD4 count and viral load, chemistries, fasting lipids, HIV resistance testing, STD and hepatitis screening, urinalysis, TB screening, and for women a Pap smear and pregnancy test. Two tests on the list are conditional on the drug being considered: HLA-B*5701 if considering abacavir, and tropism testing if considering a CCR5 antagonist. A CCR5 antagonist works only if the patient's virus enters through CCR5, so virus that uses CXCR4 or both coreceptors escapes it.

This man's physician is considering a drug that blocks CCR5, so his virus must be shown to use CCR5 before it is prescribed. Tropism is read from the envelope, where the V3 loop of gp120 is the main determinant; phenotypic assays such as Trofile test infection of CCR5-bearing versus CXCR4-bearing cells, and genotypic assays sequence the region. Skipping this step risks giving a drug that has no activity against his virus.
explain.table:
TestRequired beforeWhy
HLA-B*5701AbacavirHypersensitivity risk in carriers
Tropism assayCCR5 antagonistDrug works only against CCR5-using virus
why: HLA-B*5701 testing is required before abacavir, not before a CCR5 antagonist.
p24 antigen is a diagnostic marker in early or late disease and says nothing about coreceptor use.
TB screening is part of the baseline panel but does not decide whether this drug can work.
The diagnosis is already established, and a repeat screen gives no coreceptor information.
explain.takeaway: Before a CCR5 antagonist is prescribed, a tropism assay must show the virus uses CCR5, just as HLA-B*5701 testing must precede abacavir.
explain.topic: Baseline tests before choosing a regimen
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To describe current recommendations for HIV testing and the use of laboratory markers in patient management

questions.stem:
A reference laboratory amplifies the protease and reverse transcriptase genes from a patient's plasma and inserts them into a standard HIV backbone that lacks those genes. The resulting recombinant virus is grown in cell culture in the presence of increasing concentrations of each antiretroviral drug. For one drug, 50% inhibition of replication requires a concentration 14 times higher than that needed for a laboratory reference strain.

Which of the following best describes this result?
choices: A genotypic result showing a single point mutation
A tropism result showing CXCR4 coreceptor use
Evidence of transmitted drug resistance at infection
A direct measure of reduced drug susceptibility
A measure of the plasma viral load response to therapy

explain.html:
HIV resistance assays come in two kinds. A genotypic assay sequences the protease and reverse transcriptase genes from plasma and infers susceptibility from known mutations, an indirect measure that needs interpretation. A phenotypic assay inserts the patient's gag/protease/RT fragment into a deleted proviral clone, grows the recombinant virus in culture, and directly measures its ability to replicate in drug compared with a reference strain. The result is a fold change: the patient IC50 divided by the control IC50.

Here the patient's virus needs 14 times the reference concentration for 50% inhibition, a 14-fold change, which is a direct measure of reduced susceptibility. Because the phenotype shows the summed effect of all mutations at once, it is most useful after multiple failures when the genotype is hard to read.
explain.table:
Genotypic assayPhenotypic assay
What it measuresGene sequence (mutations)Viral growth in drug
Direct or indirectIndirect, needs interpretationDirect
ResultList of mutationsFold change in IC50 vs reference
Speed and costFaster, cheaperSlower, more expensive
why: A genotype reports sequence changes; this assay measured growth in drug.
Tropism assays test coreceptor use with envelope genes, not drug susceptibility with protease and RT genes.
Transmitted resistance describes when resistance was acquired, which a culture assay cannot tell.
Viral load is measured by quantitative RNA testing on plasma, not by culture in drug.
explain.takeaway: Phenotypic resistance assays directly measure viral growth in drug and report fold change in IC50 versus a reference strain, while genotypic assays infer susceptibility indirectly from mutations.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To have a basic understanding of HIV drug resistance & viral tropism testing

questions.stem:
A 22-year-old woman is diagnosed with HIV infection 2 months after a negative test. She has never taken any antiretroviral drug, including pre-exposure prophylaxis. A baseline genotypic resistance assay, sent before treatment, shows a mutation in the reverse transcriptase gene that confers high-level resistance to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.

Which of the following best explains this finding?
choices: She acquired a virus that was already drug resistant
A secondary mutation selected by her therapy
Resistance selected by poor adherence to treatment
Laboratory contamination by a reference strain
A tropism switch from CCR5 to CXCR4 coreceptor use

explain.html:
Resistance can arise in two ways. Acquired resistance develops in a patient on therapy when incomplete suppression selects resistant quasispecies. Transmitted drug resistance (TDR) is the transmission of drug-resistant HIV at the time of initial infection, so the patient carries resistant virus before ever taking a drug. In the START study of treatment-naive persons, TDR was present in about 10% overall and 12.6% in the USA, with NNRTI resistance the most common class in the USA (8.4%).

This woman has never taken an antiretroviral drug, including PrEP, so nothing in her body could have selected an NNRTI-resistant variant. She must have acquired a virus that was already resistant. This is why resistance testing is recommended in acute and chronic infection before therapy, so the first regimen avoids drugs the virus already escapes.
explain.table:
TermMeaning
Primary mutationSelected early; usually decreases drug susceptibility
Secondary mutationSelected after primary mutations; may have a limited effect
Transmitted drug resistanceResistant HIV transmitted at initial infection
why: Secondary mutations are selected under drug pressure after primary mutations, and she has had no drug exposure.
Adherence-related resistance requires that she be taking therapy, and she never has.
A reference strain is drug susceptible, so contamination could not create a resistance mutation.
A tropism switch changes coreceptor use and does not cause NNRTI resistance.
explain.takeaway: Drug resistance in a newly infected, treatment-naive patient is transmitted drug resistance, which is why genotypic resistance testing is done at diagnosis before therapy.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To have a basic understanding of HIV drug resistance & viral tropism testing

questions.stem:
An investigator models HIV replication in an untreated patient. The viral genome is about 10 kilobases, and the replicating enzyme introduces roughly one new mutation in every third newly infected cell. Before any drug is given, sequencing shows the plasma contains a dominant drug-susceptible population plus rare variants carrying single mutations that reduce susceptibility to several drugs. A single antiretroviral drug is then given alone.

Which of the following is the most likely outcome?
choices: Durable suppression, because resistant variants are too rare to matter
New resistance mutations induced by direct drug damage to viral RNA
Rebound of viremia as preexisting resistant variants are selected
Clearance of the virus once susceptible variants are eliminated
A permanent rise in CD4 count without any change in viral load

explain.html:
HIV reverse transcriptase is error prone: a new mutation arises in about every third newly infected cell, and with a 10 kb genome, every possible single mutation arises once a day somewhere in the body. The virus therefore exists as a swarm of quasispecies, and variants with reduced susceptibility are present before treatment begins. When therapy suppresses incompletely (inadequate potency, inadequate drug levels, inadequate adherence, or preexisting resistance), the susceptible majority falls while the resistant variants are selected and take over.

A single drug given alone is exactly that kind of incomplete suppression. The susceptible population drops, the rare preexisting resistant variants expand, and viremia rebounds. This is why therapy combines drugs from different classes, so no single mutation can rescue the virus.
why: Rare resistant variants expand quickly once the drug removes their susceptible competitors.
Drugs select variants that already exist; they do not create mutations by damaging viral RNA.
Resistant variants persist and keep replicating, so the virus is not cleared.
Without viral suppression the CD4 count does not durably recover.
explain.takeaway: Error-prone reverse transcription means resistant variants exist before treatment; any incomplete suppression, including monotherapy, selects them and leads to virologic rebound.
explain.topic: Mutation rate and selection under incomplete suppression
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To have a basic understanding of HIV drug resistance & viral tropism testing

rows.why: Rare resistant variants expand quickly once the drug removes their susceptible competitors.
rows.if_right: a fully suppressive combination regimen taken with good adherence

rows.why: Drugs select variants that already exist; they do not create mutations by damaging viral RNA.
rows.if_right: never; new mutations come from error-prone reverse transcriptase, not from the drug

rows.why: Resistant variants persist and keep replicating, so the virus is not cleared.
rows.if_right: never with current drugs; therapy suppresses HIV but does not clear it

rows.why: Without viral suppression the CD4 count does not durably recover.
rows.if_right: a patient whose viral load falls below detection on effective combination therapy

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man with HIV infection and his HIV-negative female partner ask about the risk of transmission. He has taken antiretroviral therapy daily for 3 years, and his plasma HIV RNA has been below the limit of detection on every test for the past 2 years. Neither partner has genital ulcers or another sexually transmitted infection.

Which of the following factors most strongly determines his risk of transmitting HIV to her?
choices: His CD4 count
His plasma and genital viral load
Her HLA haplotype
Whether his virus uses CXCR4
The number of years since his diagnosis

explain.html:
The lecture divides biologic determinants of sexual transmission into two sides. Acquisition factors make the exposed partner more susceptible: viral load in the index case, lack of circumcision, genital ulcers, inflammatory STDs, cervical ectopy, HLA haplotype and the CCR5 Δ32 deletion. Infectiousness factors make the person with HIV more likely to transmit: the level of blood viral load, the genital viral load, stage of infection, genital ulcers, inflammatory STDs, viral subtype, R5 tropism, and antiretroviral therapy.

This man has had undetectable plasma virus for 2 years on therapy, and neither partner has ulcers or another STI. His suppressed blood and genital viral load is the factor that drives his risk toward zero, the basis of U=U (undetectable equals untransmittable). His CD4 count and years since diagnosis matter far less than the amount of virus he carries.
explain.table:
Acquisition (partner)Infectiousness (person with HIV)
Viral load in index caseBlood and genital viral load
Lack of circumcisionStage of infection
Genital ulcers, inflammatory STDsGenital ulcers, inflammatory STDs
Cervical ectopy, HLA haplotype, CCR5 Δ32Viral subtype, R5 tropism, antiretroviral therapy
why: CD4 count reflects his immune status, not how much virus he can transmit.
HLA haplotype is a susceptibility factor on her side and does not outweigh his suppressed viral load.
R5 virus, not X4, is the phenotype tied to infectiousness, and suppressed virus is not transmitted either way.
Duration matters only through stage and viral load, and therapy has controlled his viral load.
explain.takeaway: Blood and genital viral load are the main determinants of HIV infectiousness, so durable suppression on therapy makes sexual transmission effectively zero (U=U).

explain.objective: Describe the natural history of HIV-1 infection and transmission risk

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old woman is evaluated 16 days after a condom broke during intercourse with a partner later found to have untreated HIV. She has had 3 days of fever and headache. An older third-generation antibody-only enzyme immunoassay is nonreactive. The same serum sample is then run on a fourth-generation combination immunoassay, which is reactive. Plasma HIV-1 RNA is later found to be 2.4 million copies/mL.

The discordance between the two screening assays is best explained by detection of which of the following?
choices: Viral core protein released before antibodies form
Low-avidity IgG directed against envelope gp41
Proviral DNA integrated into peripheral blood cells
Cross-reacting antibodies against the HIV-2 envelope
Reverse transcriptase activity measured within the serum

explain.html:
After infection, HIV laboratory markers appear in a fixed order. HIV RNA becomes detectable by nucleic acid testing at about 10 days, p24 antigen follows a few days later, and antibodies appear only at seroconversion. The gap between detectable virus and seroconversion is the window period, during which a third-generation antibody-only assay is negative. The fourth-generation assay detects p24 antigen as well as antibody, so it turns positive earlier and shortens the window.

This woman is 16 days out from a high-risk exposure, symptomatic, with 2.4 million copies/mL of plasma RNA, so she is in acute infection. The antibody-only test is nonreactive because she has not seroconverted, and the combination test is reactive because its antigen arm picks up p24, a viral protein that circulates before antibodies form. Recognizing this window keeps an early infection from being missed by an older assay.
explain.table:
MarkerOrder of appearanceTest that detects it
HIV RNAFirst (about day 10)Nucleic acid test (NAT)
p24 antigenSecondFourth-generation Ag/Ab immunoassay
HIV antibodyLast (seroconversion)Third-generation (and fourth-generation) immunoassay
why: Any antibody, even early low-avidity IgG, would also have made the antibody-only assay reactive.
Proviral DNA sits inside blood cells and is detected by PCR on cells, not by a serum immunoassay.
Cross-reacting HIV-2 antibodies are still antibodies and would have been seen by the antibody-only test.
Screening immunoassays detect antigen and antibody; they do not measure enzyme activity.
explain.takeaway: Fourth-generation assays detect p24 antigen, which appears before antibodies, so they are positive in the acute window when antibody-only tests are still negative; HIV RNA is the earliest marker.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To develop familiarity with the different methods used to diagnose HIV infection

rows.if_right: a reactive third-generation assay in a patient early in seroconversion

rows.if_right: a PCR test run on peripheral blood mononuclear cells

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old man has had repeated condomless sexual exposures over 10 years to a partner with untreated HIV but remains HIV-negative on every test. Researchers isolate his CD4 T cells. When exposed in culture to his partner's virus, which uses only the CCR5 coreceptor, the cells are not infected. When exposed to a laboratory strain that uses CXCR4, the cells are readily infected. Sequencing of his cells shows a homozygous 32-base-pair deletion in one host gene.

Which step of the viral life cycle is blocked in this man's cells exposed to his partner's virus?
choices: Reverse transcription of viral RNA after uncoating
Integration of proviral DNA into the host genome
Coreceptor engagement by gp120 before membrane fusion
Cleavage of Gag-Pol polyproteins during viral maturation
Budding of new virions from the host cell plasma membrane

explain.html:
HIV enters a CD4 cell in ordered steps. Envelope gp120 binds CD4 and then a coreceptor, CCR5 or CXCR4, and only after coreceptor binding does gp41 mediate fusion of viral and cell membranes. Reverse transcription, integration, assembly and budding all depend on that entry. The lecture lists the CCR5 gene Δ32 deletion among the host factors that lower the chance of acquiring HIV.

This man's cells resist his partner's CCR5-only (R5) virus but are infected by a CXCR4-using strain, and he carries a homozygous 32-base-pair deletion. Without functional CCR5, an R5 virus cannot complete coreceptor engagement, so fusion never happens and the cycle stops at entry. The CXCR4 result shows the rest of his cells' machinery works, which is why the protection applies to R5 virus and not to X4 virus.
why: Reverse transcription happens only after entry, which the R5 virus never achieves here.
Integration is downstream of entry and is the target of integrase inhibitors.
Gag-Pol cleavage by protease is a late maturation step and is unaffected by a coreceptor defect.
Budding is a late step, and the CXCR4 result shows his cells support the late cycle normally.
explain.takeaway: Homozygous CCR5 Δ32 removes the CCR5 coreceptor, blocking gp120 coreceptor binding and entry of R5-tropic HIV, while X4 virus can still enter through CXCR4.
explain.topic: CCR5 delta32 and resistance to infection
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the natural history of HIV-1 infection and transmission risk

rows.why: Reverse transcription happens only after entry, which the R5 virus never achieves here.
rows.if_right: a cell that admits the virus but contains an agent blocking RNA-to-DNA conversion, such as an NRTI or NNRTI

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old woman has had HIV infection for 12 years. She has taken the same antiretroviral regimen with excellent adherence, and her plasma HIV RNA has been below the limit of detection on every check for 6 years. Ten days ago she had a febrile respiratory illness and received an influenza vaccine at a pharmacy on the same day. A routine viral load drawn today returns 310 copies/mL. CD4 count is 690/mm3, unchanged from before.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Repeat the viral load after the recent illness and vaccination have passed
Send a genotypic resistance assay today and switch to a new three-drug regimen
Add a fourth antiretroviral drug to her current regimen
Stop therapy because her CD4 count is normal
Order a phenotypic tropism assay before any change

explain.html:
Guidelines for plasma HIV RNA testing set the schedule: two tests at baseline, a test 4 to 8 weeks after starting or changing therapy, then every 3 to 4 months on therapy. They also say do not test within 4 weeks of an acute illness or following vaccination, because a value drawn then is not a reliable read of drug activity. The goal of therapy is a viral load below the detection limit of current tests, and complete suppression is maintained to prevent resistance.

This woman has 6 years of undetectable virus, excellent adherence and an unchanged CD4 count, and her single value of 310 copies/mL was drawn 10 days after a febrile illness and a vaccine. That timing makes the result uninterpretable, so the next step is to repeat it once the 4-week window has passed. Acting on a mistimed value risks an unnecessary regimen change, while a persistent rise on repeat testing would be handled as virologic failure.
why: Resistance testing and a switch are for confirmed failure, not one value drawn inside the 4-week window.
Adding a single drug to a possibly failing regimen is not how failure is managed and is not indicated here.
Therapy is continued for life, and a good CD4 count is a reason to continue.
Tropism testing matters only when a CCR5 antagonist is being considered.
explain.takeaway: Do not interpret an HIV viral load drawn within 4 weeks of an acute illness or vaccination; repeat it before calling a low-level rise treatment failure.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To describe current recommendations for HIV testing and the use of laboratory markers in patient management

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man started his first antiretroviral regimen 7 months ago. He admits he often skipped doses during a period of unstable housing. His results are:

[[labs 0]]

He is now taking his medications reliably again.

Which of the following is the preferred test to guide the next regimen?
choices: Phenotypic tropism assay
Genotypic resistance assay
Phenotypic resistance assay
Repeat CD4 count in 3 months
HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay

explain.html:
With effective therapy and good adherence, the viral load falls steeply within weeks and is below 20 copies/mL by about 4 months. Failure to suppress, or a rebound, signals a problem, and the classic driver is incomplete suppression (inadequate potency, drug levels or adherence, or preexisting resistance), which selects drug-resistant quasispecies. Resistance testing is recommended at first regimen failure. At that point the mutation pattern is usually straightforward and easy to interpret, so the genotypic assay is preferred; it is also cheaper, faster and more sensitive. The phenotypic assay is less preferred here because it is more expensive and slower, and it becomes comparable only after multiple failures.

This man never fully suppressed, then rebounded to 24,000 copies/mL during a period of missed doses, which is first regimen failure. A genotype now identifies which drugs the selected virus can still be treated with.
explain.table:
SituationGenotypePhenotype
Primary infection or before ARTPreferred: cost-effective, rapidLess preferred: expensive, slower
First failurePreferred: simple mutation patternLess preferred
Multiple failuresComparable; consider bothComparable; shows summed effect of mutations
why: Tropism testing applies only when a CCR5 antagonist is being considered.
Phenotyping is less preferred at first failure because it is slower and more expensive.
Waiting lets viremia continue and resistance accumulate.
The differentiation assay is part of diagnosis and says nothing about drug susceptibility.
explain.takeaway: Virologic failure on a first regimen is evaluated with a genotypic resistance assay, preferred because the mutation pattern is usually simple; phenotyping becomes comparable after multiple failures.
explain.topic: Resistance testing at first regimen failure
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To have a basic understanding of HIV drug resistance & viral tropism testing

questions.stem:
A 48-year-old man has had untreated HIV infection for many years, with a slow decline in CD4 count. Stored plasma samples are analyzed. Early samples contain virus that infects only cells expressing CCR5. The most recent sample contains virus that also infects cells expressing CXCR4, and over the following year his CD4 count falls much faster than before. Sequencing of the envelope gene in the newer virus shows a higher net positive charge in one short region.

The change in the newer virus is located in which of the following?
choices: The gp41 fusion peptide
The p24 capsid protein
The V3 loop of gp120
The reverse transcriptase active site
The protease cleavage site of Gag-Pol

explain.html:
HIV uses CD4 plus a coreceptor to enter cells, and the coreceptor a virus uses is its tropism. Envelope gp120 mediates CD4 and coreceptor binding and has five conserved and five variable domains, while gp41 mediates fusion. The third variable (V3) loop of gp120, about 35 amino acids, is the primary determinant of tropism, and CXCR4 use goes with basic residues at positions 11 and 25 and a higher net positive charge. In cohort data, the transition from R5 to X4 virus is followed by a faster fall in CD4 count.

This man's early virus used only CCR5, his newer virus also uses CXCR4, his CD4 decline accelerated afterward, and the envelope change is a higher positive charge in one short region. That describes a shift in the V3 loop. Tropism matters clinically because a CCR5 antagonist cannot block virus that has learned to use CXCR4.
explain.table:
Envelope proteinRole
gp120Binds CD4 and coreceptor; V3 loop sets tropism
gp41Mediates fusion with the cell membrane
why: gp41 mediates fusion after coreceptor binding; it does not decide which coreceptor is used.
p24 is a core protein inside the virion and does not contact host receptors.
Reverse transcriptase mutations cause drug resistance, not a change in coreceptor use.
Protease cleavage affects maturation, not entry or tropism.
explain.takeaway: Emergence of CXCR4-using virus is followed by faster CD4 decline, and tropism is determined mainly by the V3 loop of gp120, where a higher net positive charge favors CXCR4 use.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To have a basic understanding of HIV drug resistance & viral tropism testing

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man with HIV and resistance to several drug classes is switched to a new regimen that includes maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist. Before the switch, the original phenotypic tropism assay reported CCR5-tropic virus. Pill counts confirm full adherence and he takes no interacting drugs. A genotypic resistance assay of protease and reverse transcriptase at 16 weeks shows the same mutations as before the switch, with no new ones.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following best explains this course?
choices: New reverse transcriptase mutations that reduce maraviroc activity
Outgrowth of a minor CXCR4-using population the assay missed
A CCR5 delta32 deletion arising in his own CD4 T cells
Missed doses that let drug-susceptible virus keep replicating
Drug resistance transmitted to him at his initial infection

explain.html:
HIV enters cells through CD4 plus a coreceptor, either CCR5 (R5 virus) or CXCR4 (X4 virus), and a CCR5 antagonist such as maraviroc works only against virus that depends on CCR5. Tropism assays decide whether that drug can be used. The original Trofile phenotypic assay detects minor X4 species only at about 5 to 10%, whereas Trofile-ES detects them at about 0.3 to 1%. When a drug suppresses the majority population but not a minority, that preexisting resistant quasispecies is selected and grows out, the same principle that drives drug resistance in general. Emergence of X4 virus is followed by faster CD4 decline.

In this man the viral load fell after the switch and then rebounded while he was fully adherent, his CD4 count dropped from 330 to 190, and the protease and reverse transcriptase genotype was unchanged. Those facts point away from new PR/RT mutations, nonadherence, or transmitted resistance and toward an X4 minority missed by the less sensitive assay that the CCR5 blockade selected.
explain.table:
AssayWhat it readsLimit
Genotypic resistance (PR/RT)Mutations in protease and reverse transcriptase genesSays nothing about coreceptor use
Original Trofile (phenotypic tropism)Pseudovirus entry into CCR5 or CXCR4 indicator cellsDetects minor X4 virus only at about 5 to 10%
Trofile-ESSame, more sensitiveDetects X4 virus at about 0.3 to 1%
why: Maraviroc targets the host CCR5 coreceptor, not reverse transcriptase, and the genotype shows no new mutations.
CCR5 delta32 is an inherited host deletion that protects against R5 virus; it is not acquired during therapy.
Pill counts confirm full adherence, so the rebound did not come from missed doses.
Transmitted resistance is present from the start and would not cause a new rebound with an unchanged genotype after a switch.
explain.takeaway: Phenotypic tropism assays have limited sensitivity for minor CXCR4-using variants; a CCR5 antagonist selects those variants, leading to viral rebound and accelerated CD4 decline.
explain.topic: Tropism assay sensitivity and selection of minor X4 virus
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: To have a basic understanding of HIV drug resistance & viral tropism testing

questions.stem:
A 37-year-old woman with newly diagnosed HIV infection starts a guideline-recommended three-drug regimen. Her baseline genotype shows drug-sensitive virus. She uses a pill-reminder app, and refill records show no missed doses. She has had no recent illness or vaccination. She is worried because her viral load is still detectable and asks whether the regimen is already failing.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and plan?
choices: Early virologic failure; send a genotypic resistance assay now
Possible switch in tropism; send a phenotypic tropism assay now
Expected response; continue and recheck viral load in 3 months
Ongoing low-level replication; switch to a new anchor drug now
Inadequate potency; add a fourth drug from a different class today

explain.html:
Plasma HIV RNA is the main marker of treatment response. Guidelines call for two viral load tests at baseline, a test 4 to 8 weeks after starting or changing therapy, and then testing every 3 to 4 months, with the goal of lowering viral load below the detection limit of current tests. In a typical responder, the viral load falls steeply in the first month and reaches an undetectable level, such as under 20 copies/mL, by about 4 months, while the CD4 count rises. Resistance testing is recommended at regimen failure, meaning persistent or rebounding viremia.

This woman's two baseline values (96,400 and 81,900) show normal variation between tests, and her 4-week value of 260 copies/mL is a more than 300-fold fall with a rising CD4 count. With full adherence and drug-sensitive virus, that is the expected response, not failure. She should continue the regimen and have the next viral load at the routine interval, expecting it to be undetectable.
explain.table:
Time pointViral load testingWhat to expect
BaselineTwo testsValues vary somewhat between tests
4 to 8 weeks on ARTOne testLarge fall, may still be detectable
Every 3 to 4 monthsOngoingBelow the detection limit (for example, under 20 copies/mL)
FailurePersistent or rebound viremiaCheck adherence; genotypic resistance testing
why: A steep fall to a low detectable level at 4 weeks is a response; genotyping is for persistent or rebounding viremia.
Tropism testing is done before starting a CCR5 antagonist, and nothing here suggests faster CD4 loss.
Switching the anchor drug responds to failure, which a falling viral load and rising CD4 do not show.
Her complete regimen is working as expected, so there is no potency problem to fix with a fourth drug.
explain.takeaway: After starting ART, viral load is checked at 4 to 8 weeks and then every 3 to 4 months; a large early fall that is still detectable is expected, and resistance testing is for persistent or rebound viremia.
explain.topic: Interpreting the early viral load response to ART
